title: Emergency Supply: Patient Request
intro: Saturday afternoon. Mrs. O'Brien is a regular patient — out of her Ramipril, her GP surgery is closed until Monday, and she has no prescription with her.

n1.text: What do you need to establish first?

choices.label: Whether this is a patient-request or prescriber-request emergency supply
choices.feedback: Right — the two routes have different rules (quantity limits, follow-up requirements), so classifying it correctly comes first.

choices.label: Whether she can pay for it privately
choices.feedback: Payment isn't the deciding factor here — the type of emergency supply request is.

choices.label: Tell her to attend the out-of-hours GP service instead
choices.feedback: For a routine repeat medication like this, an emergency supply from the pharmacy is the appropriate route.

fix1.text: This is a patient-request emergency supply — Mrs. O'Brien is asking directly, with no prescriber involved yet.

n2.text: Confirmed: patient-request. What's the maximum quantity you can supply?

choices.label: 5 days' treatment
choices.feedback: Correct — 5 days is the general limit (exceptions include smallest pack of inhalers/creams, a full course of liquid antibiotics, or a full cycle of oral contraceptives).

choices.label: A full 30-day supply
choices.feedback: 30 days is too much for a patient-request supply — that's not the rule here.

choices.label: Whatever amount she asks for
choices.feedback: The quantity is capped by law, not set by the patient's request.

fix2.text: The general rule for a patient-request emergency supply is a maximum of 5 days' treatment.

n3.text: You dispense 5 days' Ramipril. What must the label say?

choices.label: 'Emergency Supply' clearly stated
choices.feedback: Correct — any emergency supply must be clearly labelled as such.

choices.label: Nothing different from a normal label
choices.feedback: The label must flag this as an emergency supply so anyone handling the medicine afterwards knows the circumstances.

fix3.text: Every emergency supply label must clearly state 'Emergency Supply'.

end.text: Handled correctly. Because this was a patient request (not a prescriber request), there's no legal requirement for a follow-up prescription — though it's good practice to encourage Mrs. O'Brien to see her GP for a proper repeat.

title: Emergency Supply: Prescriber Request
intro: A GP phones the pharmacy directly on a Friday evening: a patient needs their epilepsy medication started urgently, but the GP can't get a paper prescription to you until Monday.

n1.text: What must the GP do as part of requesting this emergency supply?

choices.label: Undertake to provide a valid prescription within 72 hours
choices.feedback: Correct — the prescriber must undertake to supply a valid prescription within 72 hours of the request.

choices.label: Just email a photo of a prescription pad
choices.feedback: A photo isn't sufficient — a valid prescription must still follow within the set timeframe.

choices.label: Nothing further, once they've phoned
choices.feedback: The phone request must still be followed up with a valid prescription within the set timeframe.

fix1.text: The rule: the prescriber must undertake to supply a valid prescription within 72 hours of requesting the emergency supply.

n2.text: Four days pass and the GP still hasn't sent the prescription. What's the significance of the 72-hour window here?

choices.label: It's been breached — the prescriber failed their undertaking, and that should be followed up
choices.feedback: Correct. Once that window passes without the promised prescription, it's a compliance issue on the prescriber's side worth following up.

choices.label: It doesn't matter, as long as the patient got their medicine
choices.feedback: Supplying the medicine doesn't remove the prescriber's obligation to send the follow-up prescription.

fix2.text: The 72-hour undertaking is a real obligation — if it's missed, it should be followed up.

n3.text: What must the label on this supply say?

choices.label: 'Emergency Supply'
choices.feedback: Correct — this applies to all emergency supplies, patient or prescriber request.

choices.label: The GP's undertaking reference number
choices.feedback: There's no such reference number requirement — the label just needs to say 'Emergency Supply'.

fix3.text: The label requirement is simply 'Emergency Supply', clearly stated.

end.text: Handled correctly. Prescriber-request emergency supplies hinge on that 72-hour undertaking — track it, and follow up if it's missed.

title: Naloxone Without a Prescription
intro: A distressed man rushes into the pharmacy saying his friend has collapsed outside and he thinks it's an overdose. He's heard the pharmacy might have something that can help immediately.

n1.text: Can you supply and administer Naloxone here without a prescription?

choices.label: Yes, if you're a trained pharmacist and this matches its approved use
choices.feedback: Correct — trained pharmacists can supply Naloxone without a prescription, but only for its approved indication.

choices.label: No, Naloxone always requires a prescription
choices.feedback: Naloxone is one of the medicines a trained pharmacist can supply without a prescription — training is the requirement, not a prescription.

fix1.text: A trained pharmacist can supply Naloxone without a prescription, for its approved indication.

n2.text: What is Naloxone actually indicated for in this without-prescription pathway?

choices.label: Respiratory depression from known or suspected narcotic overdose
choices.feedback: Correct — that's specifically what it covers.

choices.label: Any kind of collapse or medical emergency
choices.feedback: It's specific to respiratory depression from narcotic overdose — not a general emergency medicine for any collapse.

fix2.text: Naloxone (without prescription) is specifically for respiratory depression from known or suspected narcotic overdose.

n3.text: Before any of this applies, what must be true of the pharmacist supplying it?

choices.label: They must have completed PSI-approved training
choices.feedback: Correct — this without-prescription supply route only applies once the pharmacist has completed the required training.

choices.label: Nothing — any registered pharmacist can do this automatically
choices.feedback: Training is required first — it's not automatic for every registered pharmacist.

fix3.text: PSI-approved training is required before a pharmacist can supply Naloxone this way.

end.text: If your pharmacy has a trained pharmacist on duty, Naloxone can be supplied for this indication without delay. If not, this becomes a 999 / emergency services situation instead.

title: A Prescription Outside Scope?
intro: A prescription arrives from a nurse prescriber for a medicine that seems unusual for their typical area of practice — you're not sure it's within their scope.

choices.label: Verify the prescription's validity — e.g. contact the prescriber or their collaborating doctor
choices.feedback: Correct — this is the professional obligation: verify, don't assume.

choices.label: Refuse to dispense it automatically
choices.feedback: Automatic refusal isn't correct either — you're expected to verify first, not reject outright.

choices.label: Dispense it anyway without question
choices.feedback: Dispensing without checking skips your professional obligation to verify validity.

fix1.text: The correct step is always to verify — e.g. by contacting the prescriber or their collaborating doctor — rather than assuming either way.

n2.text: You contact the prescriber and they confirm it's within their scope and clinically appropriate. What now?

choices.label: Proceed with dispensing as normal
choices.feedback: Correct — once validity is confirmed, there's no remaining barrier to dispensing.

choices.label: Still refuse, just to be safe
choices.feedback: Once you've verified and it checks out, refusing anyway isn't warranted or professional.

fix2.text: Once verification confirms the prescription is valid and appropriate, it should be dispensed as normal.

end.text: Verification — not automatic refusal or automatic compliance — is the professional standard whenever a prescription looks outside a prescriber's typical scope.
